abstract: Vaccination has been a cornerstone of public health, substantially reducing the global burden of infectious diseases, notably evident during the COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2. However, vulnerable populations (VPs), including those in extreme age groups and those with underlying health conditions, have borne a disproportionate burden of morbidity and mortality from infectious diseases. Understanding vaccine immunogenicity in these populations is crucial for developing effective vaccines. Characterizing vaccine responses in VPs presents unique challenges due to under-vaccination, sub-optimal vaccine responses, and distinct mechanisms of vaccine-induced protection. To address these challenges, experts convened at the 4th International Precision Vaccines Conference in Rome. Co-hosted by the Precision Vaccines Program of Boston Children’s Hospital and Ospedale Pediatrico Bambino Gesù, the conference focused on biomarkers of vaccine safety and efficacy in vulnerable populations. Discussions at the conference emphasized the need for multidisciplinary strategies and international collaborations to optimize vaccine development. Key areas of focus included assessing vaccine safety, defining biomarkers for vaccine immunogenicity, developing human in vitro assay models, and accelerating the selection of novel vaccine formulations and adjuvants tailored for vulnerable populations. The conference provided a platform for experts from diverse fields, including immunology, paediatrics, and vaccinology, to exchange ideas and advance research in precision vaccines. This manuscript highlights key concepts discussed at the conference and underscores the importance of precision vaccines in addressing the unique needs of vulnerable populations.
body:
1.
Introduction
Vaccination against infectious pathogens is one of the most successful and cost-effective health interventions known. This has become more evident in recent years after the spread of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS)- Coronavirus (CoV)-2, the agent that causes coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). The rapid development of COVID-19 vaccines successfully limited the severity of the disease and significantly reduced the number of hospitalizations and deaths worldwide. Despite these public health benefits, the pandemic has shown that the burden of morbidity and mortality associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection disproportionately affected the frailest and oldest people, a pattern shared by other pathogens with high pandemic potential, such as influenza viruses. Indeed, some demographic factors (pregnancy, obesity, and advanced age) and genetic features confer a heightened susceptibility to severe illness placing a priority on the study of vaccine immunogenicity and protection in distinct vulnerable populations (VPs) [
1
]. VPs include newborns, older adults as well as those affected by chronic and immune compromising medical conditions. Optimizing immunization of VPs is challenging as: a) they are often under vaccinated for various reasons, including low acceptability, uncertainty or misconceptions among patients and healthcare providers about the safety and efficacy of vaccination, cost, and access/distribution constraints [
2
]; b) they have a sub-optimal response to vaccines [
3
]; and c) VPs may have distinct mechanisms of vaccine-induced protection. Characterizing population-specific vaccine immunogenicity will inform discovery and development of novel vaccines, and entails: assessing vaccine safety in relation to vaccine-associated Adverse Events (AEs), defining biomarkers that enable quantification of vaccine immunogenicity according to host characteristics, including genetic background, defining new human in vitro assay models to test vaccine mechanisms of action with high-throughput, and accelerating and de-risking selection of novel vaccine formulations and/or adjuvants, including those specifically tailored for vulnerable populations and sub-populations.
A gathering of experts from diverse fields, including immunology, paediatrics, vaccinology, systems biology, convened in Rome on 05 and 06 October 2023, for the 4th biennial International Precision Vaccines Conference (IPVC) (
Fig. 1
). Co-hosted by the Precision Vaccines Program (PVP) of Boston Children’s Hospital (BCH; Boston, MA, United States) and
Ospedale Pediatrico Bambino Gesù
(OPBG; Rome, Italy), the
Biomarkers of vaccine safety and efficacy in Vulnerable Populations
Conference was convened by the IPVC Organizing Committee led by Prof. Ofer Levy of BCH and Prof. Paolo Palma of OPBG. The conference aimed to discuss multidisciplinary strategies and promote international collaborations in the field of vaccine development. The subsequent sections provide highlights from the conference and discuss key concepts in the field of precision vaccines.
2.
Exploring novel approaches to human vaccination: Lessons from the pandemic
We reflected on insights gained from the coronavirus pandemic and delved into innovative controlled models for human vaccination. We considered progress towards defining vaccine CoPs for both established and emerging pathogens [
4
,
5
].
Sir
Andrew J Pollard
(Director, Oxford Vaccine Group, Department of Paediatrics, University of Oxford, UK) discussed the historical context of pandemics. He highlighted the rapid response to COVID-19, leveraging existing knowledge from previous outbreaks such as SSARS and Middle Eastern Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) [
6
,
7
]. He discussed the challenges faced during the development and rollout of vaccines, including manufacturing, clinical trials, and addressing misinformation. The presentation addressed the ethical distribution of vaccines and the impact on global mortality, emphasizing the need to prioritize older adults and vulnerable populations [
8
]. Pollard also explored the effectiveness of various vaccines against severe disease and death, highlighting that despite differences in efficacy against infection, most vaccines performed similarly in preventing severe outcomes. He concluded with considerations for future pandemics, including the role of big pharma, potential microbial threats, climate change, and the need for preparedness highlighting the urgency for global collaboration, as there is still much work to be done to be adequately prepared for future pandemics.
Prof. Pierre Van Damme
(director of the Centre for the Evaluation of Vacccination @ Vaccinopolis, University of Antwerp, Belgium) discussed the importance of controlled human infection model (CHIM) studies in vaccine development for COVID-19 [
9
]. He outlined the key strengths of human challenge trials, including controlled parameters, standardized strains, and the ability to study mucosal immunity [
10
], and compared them to traditional field trials, highlighting the potential for rapid insights into transmission risks. The controlled environment of human challenge trials enables rapid assessment of vaccine efficacy and rapid selection of candidate vaccines, determination of infection doses, and understanding of the natural history of the disease. Van Damme underscored that human challenge trials are not a replacement for larger safety studies but can provide valuable information about the efficacy of candidate vaccines, especially regarding correlates of protection, mucosal immunity and transmission blocking potential [
11
].
3.
Innovations in vaccine development: Genetic analysis and immune sex differences
Prof.
Rino Rappuoli
(Scientific Director, Fondazione Biotecnopolo di Siena, Siena, Italy) delved into the transformative journey of vaccine development. Rappuoli described the challenges faced in the 1990s with vaccines developed against meningococcal strains [
12
], and notably the B strain, due to its high antigenic variability and risk of antigenic cross-reactivity with human tissues. The breakthrough came with reverse vaccinology and genomics, exemplified by Craig Venter’s work in sequencing the genome of meningococcal B [
13
]. This revolutionary approach paved the way for identifying vaccine antigens, ultimately resulting in licensed vaccines since 2013. The significance of structural biology was highlighted using the example of RSV. Jason McLellan’s work on understanding the prefusion and postfusion states of the F protein led to the data-informed selection of the prefusion form as an excellent vaccine antigen [
14
]. Rappuoli emphasized the speed and efficiency of synthetic biology, recounting the remarkable response during the H7N9 avian flu outbreak in 2013 [
15
]. The ability to rapidly synthesize genes and develop vaccines without physical viral samples showcases the power of this approach [
16
]. A glimpse into the future was provided as Rappuoli envisions a new era in vaccine development—what he terms “reverse vaccinology 2.0.” - and anticipates a shift towards digital vaccinology, where computational tools, and synthetic gene technology will play a pivotal role [
17
].
The talk by
Philip Goulder
(Professor of Immunology, Oxford University, UK) explored the impact of early life immune responses and sex differences on responses to infections and vaccines, drawing lessons from HIV [
18
–
20
]. The study conducted in South Africa focuses on a cohort of children born to HIV-positive mothers. The research investigates the prevalence of cases similar to the “Mississippi Baby” where early antiretroviral therapy led to post-treatment control [
21
–
23
]. Goulder highlighted the hypothesis that pediatric immune responses and the developmental environment may differ from adults, making early antiretroviral therapy more likely to achieve remission or cure in children [
24
]. The study also delved into sex differences, revealing a higher susceptibility to in utero infection in females and a potential protective effect in males [
25
,
26
]. Prof. Goulder discussed the transmission of interferon (IFN)-resistant viruses to females and IFN-sensitive viruses to males, indicating a nuanced immune response based on sex [
27
]. Furthermore, the study identifies 5 cases of children maintaining viral suppression despite periods of non-adherence to antiretroviral therapy, particularly in males [
101
]. These cases exhibit low viral replicative capacities, suggesting a potential connection between viral fitness, innate immune responses, and post-treatment control.
4.
Limitations of current vaccine schedules
Walter Ricciardi
(Professor of Hygiene at the Faculty of Medicine “A. Gemelli” of the Cattolica University, Rome, Italy) discussed the challenges posed by global population aging. He highlighted the changing family structure and strain on healthcare systems and advocated for recognizing vaccines as a valuable technology, stressing their role in preventing chronic and infectious diseases [
28
]. Prof. Ricciardi explored the diverse perspectives of stakeholders, including politicians, managers, healthcare professionals, religious figures, and the media and emphasized the importance of collaboration, evidence-based decision-making, and societal value in a mission-oriented approach, particularly in the context of vaccination [
29
,
30
]. Prof. Ricciardi concluded by introducing the European Mission Board for Vaccination and its working groups focused on data and evidence, beliefs and perceptions, citizen access, and harmonization.
Claire Thorne
(Professor of Infectious Disease Epidemiology, UCL Great Ormond Street Institute of Child Health, University College London, UK) presented on vaccines in pregnancy. She discussed the history of maternal immunization, focusing on vaccines such as tetanus, influenza, pertussis, and SARS-CoV-2 [
31
,
32
]. She explored the coverage rates for influenza and pertussis, emphasizing the variability among countries and the importance of clear recommendations, communication strategies, and healthcare provider recommendations in promoting vaccine uptake [
33
,
34
]. Thorne also discussed the challenges and successes in eliminating maternal and neonatal tetanus and the shift towards sustaining elimination in most countries, where high childhood coverage should ensure that pregnancies in future cohorts are already protected. Thorne also presented data on the outcomes of COVID-19 vaccination in pregnancy, emphasizing the lower odds of preterm birth and reduced SARS-CoV-2 infection incidence in vaccinated pregnant women [
35
,
36
]. The presentation touched on maternal RSV immunization, citing the MATISSE trial’s findings of the Pfizer RSVpreF vaccine’s efficacy in preventing severe RSV-associated lower respiratory tract illness in infants [
37
,
38
]. Finally, Prof. Thorne introduced ongoing and upcoming developments in maternal vaccination, including RSV and GBS vaccines [
39
,
40
]. She highlighted the impact of passive immunization on the infant’s immune response and the timing of maternal vaccination. Thorne concluded by stressing the substantial public health impact of maternal vaccination and the evolving nature of policies and recommendations in this field.
Next, Prof.
Paolo Palma
, co-host of the event delivered a talk entitled “Vaccine efficacy in individuals with primary or secondary immune deficiency”. Dr. Palma focused on progress and challenges in developing vaccines tailored to the growing population of individuals with chronic conditions requiring tailored immunization strategies [
41
]. The research highlighted variability in COVID-19 mRNA vaccine responses among patients with primary immunodeficiencies, HIV, Trisomy 21, transplants, and inflammatory bowel diseases [
42
–
46
]. He discussed how limited vaccine immunogenicity in these groups could be linked to treatments like anti-TNF biologics in IBD or immunosuppressive regimens such as mycophenolate in transplant patients. Palma also described the phenomenon of precocious immune senescence detectable in specific diseases such as HIV infection, chronic granulomatous disease or solid organ transplantation, associated with an abnormal expansion of atypical memory B cell subsets [
47
] and a reduced immunogenicity of standard vaccines, revealing suboptimal responses in certain patient cohorts [
48
–
50
]. The discussion extended to the evaluation of the immune response against the recent 4cMenB meningococcal vaccine in perinatally HIV-infected patients, highlighting differences in the fold change increase compared to the age matched healthy control group [
51
]. Prof. Palma introduced the importance of identifying biomarkers for stratifying risk and managing vaccine interventions in populations with special vaccination needs [
52
]. He focused on the importance of studying specific immune cell subsets, using innovative approaches that combine novel flow cytometry technologies with transcriptomic assays [
53
].
This session ended with Dr.
Amy Sherman
’s talk (Adult Infectious Diseases, Brigham & Women’s Hospital and the PVP Boston, MA; USA) focused on vaccines in oncology patients. Dr. Sherman highlighted the challenges of immunosuppression and focused on strategies to optimize immunogenicity in immunocompromised oncology patients, addressing issues of vaccination timing, additional booster doses, suitable vaccine platforms or adjuvants, mAbs, and adaptive transfer from donors to recipients who undergo hematopoietic stem cell transplantation [
54
,
55
]. She emphasized the need for further research in mechanisms, pathways, and large-scale clinical trials to determine the efficacy and safety of these strategies. Dr. Sherman presented research findings on a heterologous boosting strategy using the protein adjuvanted Novavax COVID-19 vaccine after prime immunization with mRNA COVID-19 vaccines, showing some promise but acknowledging the need for more investigation [
56
]. She also explored the concept of adaptive transfer in allogeneic stem cell transplant recipients and how it might impact vaccine schedules for both the donors and recipients [
57
,
58
]. She underscored the importance of understanding host characteristics and CoPs in immunocompromised patients [
59
].
5.
New strategies to optimize vaccine efficacy
Prof. Ofer Levy
, one of the IPVC conference co-hosts and Director of the PVP, presented on
Precision vaccines: bringing precision medicine to vaccinology
. Prof. Levy discussed precision vaccines and the need for tailoring vaccines for VPs. He emphasized the impact of vaccines on preventing illnesses, hospitalizations, and deaths. The PVP focuses on intentional diversity in targeted clinical trials, utilizing multi-omics analysis to correlate vaccine responses with clinical outcomes. Levy outlined the program’s human in vitro modeling approach, accounting for age- and sex-specific responses in studying innate and adaptive immunity. The PVP also identifies small molecules, termed PVP molecules (310 potential PVP adjuvants in curated library portfolio), activating innate immune receptors for potential use in adjuvanted vaccines (i.e. opioid vaccine, influenza vaccine and DTaP vaccine). The talk delved into the role of the BCG vaccine beyond preventing tuberculosis, its impact on reduction of all-cause mortality, and the program’s work on characterizing different licensed BCG formulations [
60
–
62
]. Levy discussed the response to the COVID-19 pandemic, collaborating on biomarker studies and developing an Alum:CpG adjuvanted SARS-CoV2 vaccine optimized for older adults [
63
,
64
], which contributed to the intellectual basis underlying the
Corbevax
vaccine that is currently used in India. The speaker emphasized the importance of vaccine safety at every stage of development and highlighted the PVP’s involvement in understanding biomarkers for vaccine-associated adverse events through international collaboration [
65
,
66
]. Prof. Levy concluded by stressing the critical role of vaccinology in public health, advocating for increased funding to address societal needs effectively.
Prof. Ivan Zanoni
(BCH, Harvard Medical School, Boston, United States) discussed innate immunity, adjuvants, and vaccines. Zanoni’s lab focuses on understanding innate immunity and its role in shaping adaptive immune responses. The Zanoni Lab uses components of the
Candida albicans
fungus, specifically mannans, as adjuvants [
67
]. They demonstrated that the physical differences between mannans and other components of the fungal cell wall, such as beta-glucans, lead to distinct immune responses. The
C. albicans
mannan is small and soluble and can reach directly the draining lymph node (dLN) without inducing any inflammation in the periphery. In contrast, beta-glucans drive inflammation in the periphery and migration to the dLN of dendritic cells. In a series of elegant studies, Prof. Zanoni showed that direct draining to the dLN of the mannan induces an interferon response that allows the expansion of the dLN and the accrual of T and B lymphocytes. Zanoni also introduced a modified adjuvant called “Mannadjuvant” which combines alum hydroxide and the
C. albicans
mannan. This formulation was designed to target both the dLN and the phagocytes present at the site of the injection. When the Mannadjuvant was utilized in combination with the spike protein from SARS-CoV-2, a potent B cell response was induced. The level of neutralizing antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 were potently upregulated. Using a phage-display technology, Prof. Zanoni also proved that the repertoire of antibodies induced by the Mannadjuvant was more diverse compared to other adjuvants currently utilized in vaccine that are FDA approved. In another set of experiments that utilize recombinant hemagglutinins (HAs) from influenza A virus (IAV), Prof. Zanoni proved the capacity of the Mannadjuvant to induce antibodies that cross-react and protect against strains of IAVs whose HA were not contained in the vaccine mixture [
67
].
6.
Bioinformatic approaches to define vaccine correlates of protection
This session explored the role of T regulatory cells (Treg) in vaccine effectiveness across various health conditions, discussed the importance of collaborative data approaches in multi-institutional research and considered integration of multiomic data in precision medicine, including to advance vaccine biomarkers by using artificial intelligence techniques.
Prof. Scott J. Tebbutt
(University of British Columbia; Centre for Heart Lung Innovation, St. Paul’s Hospital, Vancouver, Canada) emphasized Treg cells in vaccine projects and diverse health conditions [
68
]. Focusing on hepatitis B and herpes zoster vaccines, he presented evidence supporting Tregs’ role in predicting vaccine effectiveness [
69
,
70
]. Insights from asthma, diabetes and heart transplantation studies revealed involvement of Treg cells in inflammatory responses and acute rejection monitoring [
71
,
72
]. The research integrated omics data, highlighting Tregs’ potential as vaccine biomarkers.
Joanne Diray-Arce
(Harvard Medical School; Data Management and Analysis Core (DMAC), PVP, BCH, Boston, United States) discussed the importance of collaborative data approaches in multi-institutional vaccine and infectious disease research [
73
]. Emphasizing the significance of data management and governance, she highlighted the challenges in multi-institutional research, including diverse data resources, security concerns, and ethical considerations. Dr. Arce detailed her involvement in the Human Immunology Project Consortium (HIPC). She described large-scale projects such as the Expanded Program on Immunization Consortium and the COVID-19 cohort, involving extensive collection of biological samples and generation of substantial amounts of data. The talk delved into data quality assessments, harmonization, standardization, and the development of a computational platform for streamlined data integration [
74
,
75
]. Dr. Arce also introduced the Immune Vista Platform, facilitating centralized curation, storage, and analysis of de-identified omics data (
www.immunevista.org
). Several impactful publications resulting from the analysis of large datasets were highlighted, showcasing insights into immune responses and clinical outcomes in vaccine studies and COVID-19 cohorts [
63
,
76
–
78
]. The speaker emphasized the importance of data deposition and adherence to principles like FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable). She encouraged researchers to contribute to public deposition platforms, such as National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID)’s ImmPort database (
https://immport.niaid.nih.gov/home
).
Prof. Jessica Lasky-Su
(Harvard Medical School and Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, United States) emphasized the importance of developing vaccine biomarkers. She used the example of developing a biomarker for biological aging, termed ‘EMRage’ (electronic medical record age). Utilizing machine learning and neural networks (referred to as A.I.), she demonstrated the process of creating this biomarker by incorporating clinical data from the Mass General Brigham Biobank. She explained the importance of reproducibility and clinical relevance in biomarkers, showcasing the robustness of EMRage and its correlation with mortality prediction. Prof. Lasky-Su then transitioned to the concept of vaccine response biomarkers, highlighting the potential to predict vaccine response using A.I. with clinical data, and measures that might provide more information on vaccine response, such as specific antibodies. Prof. Lasky-Su introduced the concept of “OMICmAge” (omic DNA methylation age) as a synthesis of multiomic data recoded as DNAmethylation, demonstrating its robustness and clinical relevance. She emphasized the importance of generalizability and highlighted the diagnostic power of OMICmAge in predicting mortality and the reproducibility of her findings across diverse populations. Prof. Lasky-Su concluded by visualizing the future potential of composite vaccine response biomarkers, detailing a framework within the electronic medical record (EMR) for predicting individual responses and potential adverse events. To summarize, the presentation suggested significant potential for advancing vaccine biomarker development, leveraging A.I., multi-omic integration, and clinical data for more precise predictions and understanding of individual responses.
Among the abstracts submitted to the conference for evaluation, the most promising ones were selected for oral presentation. Among these, the abstract: A systems immunology study to assess the impact of early-life antibiotic exposure on infant vaccine immune responses by
Prof. David Lynn
(South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute (SAHMRI) and Flinders University College of Medicine and Public Health, Adelaide, Australia) was selected. Prof. Lynn presented a prospective study investigating the impact of early-life antibiotic exposure on infant vaccine immune responses [
79
]. The study recruited over 250 infants, collecting various samples for a comprehensive assessment including assessing IgG responses to >20 different vaccine antigens, shotgun metagenomic sequencing of >400 stool samples to profile the composition of the infant microbiota including at the time of vaccination and whole blood transcriptomics to assess the transcriptional response to vaccination. Preclinical models using germ-free mice and probiotic administration demonstrated the potential to rescue impaired vaccine responses (Ryan et al., In review).
7.
Vaccine safety
By meticulously assessing and monitoring the safety of vaccines, we can instill public confidence in immunization programs, ultimately preventing the spread of infectious diseases. Furthermore, robust vaccine safety practices facilitate early detection and management of adverse events, contributing to the continuous improvement of vaccine formulations and administration protocols. Overall this section highlighted current efforts in the study of adversomics.
Prof. Karina A Top
(University of Alberta, Edmonton, Alberta, INSIS) presented on the International Network of Special Immunization Services (INSIS), a global network established to advance vaccine safety through elucidating biological mechanisms of rare adverse events of special interest (AESIs) [
66
]. Such rare AESIs, occurring in fewer than one in 10,000 to 1 in >1 million individuals after vaccination are typically only identified after vaccine implementation [
80
]. INSIS employs multi-omics approaches, integrating clinical and systems biology data, termed ‘adversomics’ [
81
]. The network employs a case-control design, collecting samples and clinical data from individuals with adverse events and both vaccinated, unaffected controls and individuals with similar clinical conditions not associated with vaccination. The aim is to define molecular pathways, identify predictive biomarkers, and improve understanding of vaccine safety. The study focuses on adverse events associated with COVID-19 vaccines, such as myocarditis, pericarditis, and thrombosis with thrombocytopenia syndrome. INSIS collaborates with various partners globally and has established a data management platform for harmonized data collection and analysis. INSIS is working on protocols for prospective sample collection and engaging with partners to address gaps in surveillance, especially in low and middle-income countries. The INSIS network aims to establish a product-agnostic global platform to study mechanisms and identify biomarkers for adverse events. The results obtained from the study can inform risk-benefit assessments of new vaccines and contribute to the development of safer vaccines for future pandemic threats.
Dr. Donato Amodio
(OPBG, University of Rome “Tor Vergata” Rome, Italy) presented data from OPBG on vaccine-related myocarditis after COVID-19 vaccination [
82
]. The speaker discussed a cohort of patients admitted to the emergency department with symptoms meeting criteria for myocarditis after COVID-19 vaccination. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was employed to evaluate myocardial lesions, highlighting the importance of conducting cardiac MRI for accurate diagnosis, particularly as MRI findings closely correlated with troponin values. The patients generally showed clinical recovery with the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, amiodarone, and enalapril [
83
]. However, some patients experienced relapsing myocarditis after initial recovery, highlighting the need for ongoing follow-up [
84
]. Immunological analysis was conducted on the patients, comparing them with a cohort of children with Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children who had cardiac involvement. The analysis revealed differential expressions of proteins related to stress-induced cardiomyocyte damage, cardiac oxidative stress, and cardiac damage in myocarditis patient. Notably, these patients showed high levels of certain proteins even after six months. The study also explored the role of androgens, showing increased levels of testosterone and androstenedione in patients experiencing post-vaccine myocarditis. The elevated androgen levels persisted over time, suggesting a potential link between androgens and myocarditis [
85
]. In conclusion, the presentation emphasized the importance of continued vaccination against COVID-19, as the risk-benefit balance remains in favor of vaccination and the need for larger cohort studies and systems biology approaches.
In this session the abstract selected for oral presentation was authored by Prof.
Nigel Crawford
(Murdoch Children’s Research Institute, Royal Children’s Hospital, Department of Paediatrics, University of Melbourne) who delivered a talk about “Melbourne Children’s COVID-19 biobanking platform: biomarkers for vaccine response and adversomics”. He highlighted the challenges faced due to strict lockdown measures in Victoria during the COVID-19 pandemic. The presentation covered various aspects, including genetic predictors of adverse events post-vaccination, such as a hyperinflammatory state associated with a specific mutation [
86
,
87
]. Prof. Crawford presented studies on febrile seizures and genetic risk factors, emphasizing the importance of clinical follow-up for individuals with a history of adverse reactions to vaccines [
88
]. He discussed the impact of pandemic response measures on vaccine trials and the initiation of research projects focusing on COVID-19, transmission studies, and immune response in pediatric populations. The talk included information on biobanking initiatives related to COVID-19 vaccines, particularly in special risk groups and those experiencing adverse events like myocarditis. Prof. Crawford provided insights into ongoing research, including the collection of samples for further analysis, especially concerning myocarditis cases. He also discussed efforts to establish a national virtual biobank to facilitate data sharing and collaboration.
8.
Host-related mechanisms of suboptimal immune responses to vaccines
Considerable interindividual variability exists in immune responses to vaccination, impacting both effectiveness and duration of immunity. Indeed, a notable number of vaccine-preventable infections arise in vaccinated individuals. Various individual factors, including age, sex, genetic makeup, and underlying health conditions, play a role in determining the depth and breadth of vaccine response [
89
].
Prof. Hanno Steen
(Department of Pathology, BCH and Harvard Medical School) discussed advancements in technology, focusing on development of a mass spectrometry-based deep, affordable and scalable sample-sparing plasma proteomics pipeline. The challenges in plasma proteomics include high complexity, large dynamic range, and a wide range of physical-chemical properties, making it expensive and lacking in processing capacity. The lab’s effort has been the development of methods for deep and rapid analysis of small volumes of plasma. In 2015, the lab participated in the NIH-supported Human Immunology Project Consortium (HIPC) effort studying about 1500 plasma samples from >700 newborns, revealing extensive changes in the plasma proteome during the first week of life with emphasis on the first 48 h of life. Building on the plasma proteomics experience gained during the HIPC study, Steen’s lab developed a novel plasma proteomics pipeline for high throughput deep proteome mapping to analyze the thousands of plasma samples collected under the auspice of the U.S. NIH-sponsored Immunophenotyping of a COVID-19 Cohort (IMPACC) study to define molecular immunophenotypes associated with COVID severity and outcome. This effort was scaled for the analysis of 10,000 plasma samples from patients with various severity levels. They highlighted improvements in accuracy and dynamic information, providing insights into protein trajectories and changes over time. This novel high-throughput plasma proteomics pipeline was presented, utilizing a cost-effective method for depleting abundant plasma proteins, proving reproducibility, affordability, and compatibility with various body fluids including saliva, urine, plasma, serum, and tracheal aspirate samples.
Dr. Asimenia Angelidou
(Department of Neonatology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center; PVP, BCH; Harvard Medical School, Boston, United States) discussed challenges in early life immunization. Limited or no vaccines are available for common neonatal pathogens like
Streptococcus agalactiae
(Group B streptococcus). Safety concerns, global variations in licensed formulations, and deferred vaccinations contribute to delayed immunization or lack thereof. Factors influencing early life vaccine responses include prenatal factors (maternal immunity, and vaccination, infections), birth factors (microbiome, colonization, infections during labor), and postnatal factors (vaccine type, route, timing). The US immunization schedule reveals limited early life immunization, creating a vulnerability window from birth to 9-12 months. The World Health Organization recommends vaccines for hepatitis B, polio, and BCG. Hepatitis B vaccine aims to prevent perinatal transmission, with various formulations available. Polio vaccines, including bivalent oral polio vaccine (OPV) and inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), have diverse schedules globally, while OPV is being phased out globally. BCG, a live attenuated
Mycobacterium bovis
vaccine, is crucial in tuberculosis-endemic regions, preferably administered soon after birth [
62
]. The talk emphasized heterologous/”off-target” effects of live vaccines, particularly BCG, showcasing broader protection against infection beyond the vaccine’s antigenic target. Dr. Angelidou described ongoing research using human in vitro modeling, particularly a human monocyte training assay, to characterize off-target immunologic vaccine effects [
90
] and presented data on distinct immunometabolic responses of neonatal monocytes to BCG in vitro. In conclusion, Dr. Angelidou highlighted challenges surrounding early life vaccination and potential solutions, such as tailored adjuvants, maternal immunization, and leveraging the immune priming effects of live vaccines in vaccine development.
Dr. Nicola Cotugno
(OPBG, University of Rome “
Tor Vergata
” Rome, Italy) discussed both previous evidence on pre-vaccination signatures of immunogenicity in HIV infected children [
48
,
52
,
91
–
93
] and novel investigations performed in a multi cohort of immune-compromised children and adolescents. In particular, previous evidence in HIV-infected were presented and showed pre-vaccination transcriptional signatures able to inform on H1N1 immunogenicity after trivalent inactivated Influenza vaccination. Such results were used also to develop an in vitro gene expression testing (IVIGET), particularly informative in T follicular helper cells and B cells after in vitro stimulation with H1N1 peptides, which identified a score correlating with long-term immune responses [
91
,
93
,
94
]. The focus of the talk then shifted on the research studies made over the SARS-CoV-2 vaccination campaign in VPs. A study involving different immunocompromised cohorts (CONVERS study) highlighted distinct immune responses, especially among solid organ transplant recipients, who exhibited lower immunogenicity rates [
42
–
46
]. Pre-vaccination characteristics, especially in B-cell subsets, were crucial predictors of the vaccine response in solid organ transplanted patients. The study further explored in vitro gene expression testing at the transcriptional level and employed machine learning to develop a predictive model for vaccine immunogenicity [
52
]. The ultimate goal is to provide clinicians with a simple yet effective scoring system for vaccination decision-making.
Dr. David J. Martino
’s abstract entitled “Host-related genomic factors influencing vaccine mediated immunity” was selected for oral presentation in this section. Dr. Martino (Wal-yan Respiratory Research Centre, Telethon Kids Institute, University of Western Australia, West Perth, Western Australia, Australia) discussed the importance of understanding host-related factors influencing vaccine responses, especially in cases where individuals suffer breakthrough infection despite vaccination. He emphasized the complexity of vaccine response variations, driven by a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Focusing on genetic markers, the speaker explored >200 genetic associations related to responses to various vaccines, with HLA genes being prominent. These genetic markers are also identified as disease risk loci, revealing a connection between vaccine responsiveness and general health. To harness this information effectively, Dr. Martino proposes the use of polygenic risk scores, highlighting their success in predicting baseline risks for various conditions. While current polygenic risk scores cover numerous human traits, none have been developed for vaccine responsiveness, presenting an opportunity for impactful research. Dr. Martino also delved into the role of epigenetic biomarkers. He introduced the concept of using epigenetic biomarkers to match disease-associated signatures to adjuvant-associated signatures, providing a potential platform for precision vaccine development.
9.
Updates on RSV immunization
The last section of the conference spotlighted respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) immunization with a series of talks delivered by
Kirsten Maertens
(Centre for the Evaluation of Vaccination @ Vaccinopolis, University of Antwerp, Belgium) and
Paul Heath
(St. Georges University, London, UK) delving into the current status and providing critical insights on maternal and infant vaccination, and comparative strategies.
Prof. Maertens discussed the importance of vaccination in pregnancy. The speaker underscored RSV as leading cause of viral lower respiratory tract infections in children <5 years of age, with most severe clinical manifestations seen in infants. To protect infants from severe RSV-related outcomes, vaccinating pregnant women against RSV can be crucial as this strategy provides passive protection to the newborn from immediately after birth up to 6 months of age. The Novavax vaccine, the first RSV candidate vaccine developed for pregnant women was an RSV F-protein Recombinant Nanoparticle vaccine. This candidate, initially promising, failed to meet primary efficacy endpoints [
38
]. Therefore, subsequent RSV candidate vaccines for pregnant women from GSK and Pfizer focused on the prefusion form of RSV [
95

96
]. On the other hand, the Pfizer vaccine was effective against severe RSV-associated disease but a statistically significant numerical imbalance in the number of premature births between the vaccine and placebo group was seen in upper-middle income countries. At the end of the presentation, Prof. Maertens outlined future challenges for RSV maternal vaccination, such as researching safety, co-administration with other vaccines during pregnancy, the impact on breast milk composition, optimal timing of vaccination, and acceptance by pregnant women. Prof. Heath discussed the status of RSV immunization for infants. Strategies for pediatric RSV prevention include passive immunization through both mAbs and maternal vaccination, or active immunization of infants with pediatric RSV vaccines. Passive immunization with mAbs, has reduced hospital admissions and deaths but has limitations, including substantial cost and requiring monthly injections [
98
]. Regarding RSV vaccines for children, the speaker mentioned RNA vaccine candidates like Moderna’s (
https://classic.clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05743881
), protein-based vaccines like Advaccine’s G protein-focused vaccine [
99
], and live attenuated vaccines showing promise in early-stage trials [
100
]. Prof. Heath discussed the strengths and limitations of various RSV immunization approaches, emphasizing considerations like acceptability, coverage, immunological differences, protection duration, costs, and safety. He highlighted the challenges in comparing phase three efficacy trials due to differing definitions, populations, and control rates. Heath proposed adaptive trials with head-to-head comparisons of strategies, including maternal RSV vaccines versus infant monoclonal antibodies and combined interventions. A proposed trial would randomize pregnant women to receive infant monoclonal antibodies, maternal vaccines, or both. This adaptable platform aims to address future vaccine needs and focus on vaccines for pregnant women, a historically neglected area.
